newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania set for more talks on election law.
newsitem.headline: Albania set for more talks on election law.

text.p: Albanian politicians on Monday missed a deadline to agree a new election law and Western officials said talks would go into another round on Tuesday.

The law is aimed at paving the way for elections next month, seen as vital to stop the country sliding into a fresh bout of the rioting which broke out in February and March after the collapse of pyramid investment schemes.

Although the country is far quieter now, sporadic violence and killings continue. Volleys of automatic fire can be heard every night in the capital and a curfew reigns everywhere from nine in the evening to five in the morning.
Under a political deal brokered by European envoy Franz Vranitzky and signed by the 10 main political parties, the election law was to have been approved on Monday.

The deal says the law should be passed by parliament this week to allow President Sali Berisha to announce the election day by May 15. Under Albanian law, the president must call an election at least 45 days before voting takes place.

An official from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) said the parties still disagreed on how many seats to decide by a proportional vote and how many under a majority system in the new law.
He told Reuters that the talks would continue on Tuesday and hoped that the question would be decided then.

The dispute between Berisha's Democratic Party and the rest of the nine-party Government of National Reconciliation over the division of proportional representation and majority voting has threatened to scupper the planned elections.
The Democrats wanted most of the seats to be chosen by simple majority vote, as in the last elections in May 1996 when they won 122 of the 140 seats in parliament.
International observers said the vote was flawed and the opposition Socialists pulled out on the last day.
The rest of the government wants more seats on a proportional basis to give smaller parties seats in parliament.

An official of the Democratic Party said a compromise was emerging to have 115 seats decided by a majority vote and others on a proportional system. He also said that the number of parliamentary seats may be increased from the present 140.
"A conclusion will be reached," the official said.

The other main obstacle to the elections is the so-called Salvation Committees, groups which sprang up in several towns during the violence, mainly in the south of the country, to protect local citizens and restore some kind of order.

The political contract says the Committees must be disbanded no later than May 14, 46 days before the planned election. But the Committees say they plan to hold a meeting to decide their future only on May 16.
